common_name: Shiranami Saxifrage (Double White Fall-Blooming Woodland Saxifrage)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Shiranami is a double-flowered selection of the fall-blooming woodland saxifrage, distinct from the single-flowered species and from the related, more commonly grown Saxifraga fortunei.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich soil with reliable drainage in a sheltered, shaded spot protected from afternoon sun and drying wind. Shiranami forms low mounds of rounded, glossy leaves and sends up airy branched sprays of small, fully double white flowers from late summer into fall, well after most woodland perennials have finished blooming. Keep the soil evenly moist through the growing season and mulch lightly over winter in the colder part of its range to protect the crown. Divide congested clumps in early spring only when necessary, since this species resents frequent disturbance.

common_name: Miss Jekyll Periwinkle (Compact White-Flowered Lesser Periwinkle)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or divisions 10-15 inches apart in spring or fall in average, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Miss Jekyll is a noticeably more compact, tidier grower than the plain white-flowered 'Alba', named for the English garden designer who popularized it.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, where it forms a dense, low mat of small, dark green leaves. Miss Jekyll produces abundant pure white, pinwheel-shaped flowers in spring with light rebloom into summer, and its finer, more restrained scale suits small woodland beds, troughs, and plantings around dwarf conifers better than larger-growing periwinkle selections. It spreads by rooting stems but stays notably better-behaved and slower to wander than the species. Shear lightly after the main spring flush to keep the mat dense and encourage repeat bloom.

common_name: Alba Plena Periwinkle (Double White-Flowered Lesser Periwinkle)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or divisions 12-18 inches apart in spring or fall in average, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Alba Plena is a slower-spreading, double-flowered counterpart to the single white 'Alba' and is harder to source commercially.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; established plantings tolerate the dry shade under mature trees where turf and many perennials struggle. Alba Plena bears fully double, pure white flowers over the same glossy, trailing evergreen foliage as common periwinkle, giving a fuller, more textured bloom than the single-flowered white forms, though it fills in more slowly and stays a bit more compact. Bloom is concentrated in mid-spring with occasional scattered flowers later in the season. Because it spreads less vigorously than the species, it is better suited to small defined beds than large-scale naturalizing.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or divisions 10-15 inches apart in spring or fall in average, well-drained soil in bright partial shade; Honeydew's chartreuse foliage colors best with some filtered morning light and can green out in deep shade.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in bright, dappled partial shade rather than deep shade, since some filtered light keeps the foliage color at its brightest. Honeydew forms a dense, low mat of small, glossy, oval leaves in a distinctive chartreuse that brightens shaded ground more dramatically than the plain green species, topped by the typical lavender-blue pinwheel flowers in spring. The lighter foliage color makes it a useful accent when paired with darker-leaved shade groundcovers rather than planted as a large solid block. Trim back wandering stems in early spring to maintain a tidy, dense carpet.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension Plant Toolbox

common_name: Indigo Frost Heucherella (True Dwarf Purple-Leaved Foamy Bells)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Indigo Frost is a true dwarf selection, notably smaller in scale than most heucherella cultivars, making it a good fit for edging and small containers.

directions: Plant in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, keeping the shallow crown from drying out during summer heat. Indigo Frost forms a tight, diminutive mound of sharply cut, deep purple leaves overlaid with a silvery veil across the surface, a scale and color combination that sets it apart from the larger, more sprawling heucherella cultivars typically offered. Small sprays of pale flowers rise just above the foliage in late spring but play a minor role next to the foliage color. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to keep the compact habit from thinning out.

common_name: Gold Cascade Heucherella (Trailing Gold Foliage with Red Center)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Gold Cascade is a trailing selection bred to spill over container edges and low walls rather than form a mound.

directions: Plant in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, and give it room to trail rather than crowding it against upright neighbors. Gold Cascade produces scalloped, gold foliage with a dramatic red-flushed center that spreads outward on pliable, spilling stems, a trailing habit unlike the mounding form typical of most heucherella cultivars. Short spikes of light coral flowers appear in mid-spring above the foliage. Its cascading growth makes it especially well suited to raised containers, hanging baskets, and the tops of shaded retaining walls where the stems can drape freely.

common_name: Silver Streak Allegheny Spurge (Silver-Marked Native Pachysandra)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container clumps in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Silver Streak holds its silver leaf markings through winter more reliably than the straight species, whose mottling is often subtler and more seasonal.

directions: Plant divisions or container specimens in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade. Silver Streak is a selection of the native Allegheny spurge chosen for its consistently bold silver mottling, which emerges on new leaves in spring and intensifies through the season, holding into winter on the semi-evergreen foliage even in colder parts of its range. Small, fragrant white to pink flower spikes open at ground level in early spring just before the new leaves expand. It spreads slowly by rhizome into a refined, weed-suppressing patch, making it a good companion for hellebores, trillium, and other slow-colonizing woodland natives.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery starts in spring or fall in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Superstar was originally found and distributed as Norman Singer's Form before being renamed for retail sale, and is distinguished by larger flowers held on shorter stems than the species.

directions: Plant in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to dappled woodland light. Superstar produces noticeably larger, brighter yellow, five-petaled star-shaped flowers than the wild species, carried on shorter stalks that keep the display sitting close to the foliage rather than floating above it. First distributed among rock garden enthusiasts as Norman Singer's Form before its renaming, it flowers heavily from spring into early summer with scattered rebloom in cooler fall weather. It forms a low, spreading mat well suited to woodland path edges and small-scale groundcover plantings beneath deciduous shrubs.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension Plant Toolbox
